title: You Keep Praying for More Money. What Would More Money Reveal About the Heart You Already Have?
paragraphs: You Keep Praying for More Money. What Would More Money Reveal About the Heart You Already Have?
Maybe the question is not whether God can put more money in your hands. Maybe the frightening question is what more money would uncover in your heart.
You have prayed about the bills.
You have stared at numbers that refuse to cooperate.
You have watched prices rise while your income seemed determined to stay exactly where it was.
Maybe you have whispered prayers in the car before walking into work.
“Lord, I just need a breakthrough.”

Maybe you have prayed for the business to grow. For the promotion. For more clients. For the debt to disappear. For enough money that you can finally stop feeling that knot in your stomach every time another expense arrives.
And there is nothing inherently sinful about asking God to provide.
Jesus Himself taught His disciples to pray for daily bread.
But there is a question we do not ask nearly as often.
What if God gave you more?
Not a little more.
A lot more.
What would it reveal?
Because money does something strange to the human heart.
Sometimes money does not create the person we become.
Sometimes it simply gives the person we already are more room to come out.
If I am generous with little, greater resources may give generosity a larger reach.
If I am proud with little, greater resources may give pride a larger stage.
If I secretly measure my worth by what I own, more money may not heal that wound. It may simply give me more expensive ways to hide it.
If I already struggle to trust God when I have little, I may discover that having more creates an entirely different temptation:
trusting God less because I no longer feel that I need Him.
And suddenly the prayer changes.
“God, give me more” becomes:
“God, before You put more into my hands, show me what is already living inside my heart.”
That is where Paul's words to Timothy become painfully relevant.
He writes:
The thought of 1 Timothy 6:6 is startling: godliness joined with contentment is itself great gain.
Notice what Paul does.
He takes the language of profit and turns it upside down.
The Greek word πορισμός (porismos) carries the idea of gain or means of gain. Yet Paul refuses to let material accumulation define what “gain” ultimately means.
He points instead to εὐσέβεια μετὰ αὐταρκείας—godliness with contentment.
That word αὐτάρκεια (autarkeia) speaks of sufficiency or contentment.
Paul is confronting a lie humanity has believed for centuries:
“If I could finally get enough, I would finally become okay.”
But how much is “enough”?
That is the terrifying elasticity of greed.
Enough moves.
You once prayed for the salary you now complain about.
You once dreamed of owning something you now barely notice.
You once thought reaching a certain financial level would finally make you secure.
Then you reached it...
and discovered another level.
Another purchase.
Another comparison.
Another definition of success.
Another person online whose life suddenly made yours feel small.
The finish line moved again.
Paul continues by reminding us of something no financial adviser can change:
We entered this world carrying nothing, and we will carry nothing material out of it.
Your first breath came without a bank account.
Your final breath will not negotiate with your net worth.
One day somebody else will own the things you sacrificed years of your life to obtain.
The house will belong to someone else.
The clothes will be removed from the closet.
The accounts will be transferred.
The possessions will be divided.
The titles will disappear.
The numbers that once made you feel powerful will remain on earth while your soul stands before God.
That does not make money meaningless.
It puts money in its proper place.
Money is a tool.
Money can feed a child.
Money can support a family.
Money can fund ministry.
Money can help a struggling neighbor.
Money can employ people.
Money can provide medicine.
Money can print Bibles.
Money can support missionaries.
Money can build businesses that serve people honestly.
Money can create extraordinary opportunities for generosity.
Scripture does not teach that possessing money automatically makes someone wicked.
Abraham possessed great wealth.
Job possessed great wealth and, after enormous suffering, received great material restoration.
There were people with resources who supported Jesus' ministry.
Joseph of Arimathea was a wealthy disciple.
The problem is not that money exists in your hand.
The question is whether money has captured your heart.
That distinction matters because 1 Timothy 6:10 is frequently misquoted.
Paul does not simply say, “Money is the root of all evil.”
The Greek text says:
“ῥίζα γὰρ πάντων τῶν κακῶν ἐστιν ἡ φιλαργυρία...”
The crucial word is φιλαργυρία (philargyria): love of money.
Paul's warning is directed at an affection.
A craving.
A heart allegiance.
Money can sit quietly inside a wallet while the love of money builds an altar inside the soul.
And poor people are not automatically immune.
You do not have to possess a million dollars to worship a million dollars.
A person can have almost nothing and still organize their entire imagination around becoming rich.
A person can resent everyone who has more.
A person can fantasize about wealth as salvation.
A person can believe, “If I had their money, then I would matter.”
That is why this passage reaches far beyond wealthy Christians.
It reaches the exhausted father wondering how he will pay next month's rent.
It reaches the ambitious entrepreneur praying for expansion.
It reaches the employee desperate for promotion.
It reaches the young believer dreaming of becoming successful.
It reaches the Christian scrolling through social media, comparing houses, vacations, clothes, cars, careers and lifestyles.
It reaches the wealthy believer with investments spread across multiple accounts.
It reaches the person reading this article while secretly thinking:
“If God would just give me more money, everything would finally be okay.”
Maybe some things really would become easier.
We should not romanticize poverty.
Financial hardship can be crushing.

Debt can produce enormous pressure. Food insecurity is real. Medical expenses are real. Unemployment is real. Parents lying awake wondering how they will provide for their children are not experiencing an imaginary problem.
Christian contentment does not require pretending suffering feels pleasant.
And asking God for provision is biblical.
But Scripture refuses to let provision become our Savior.
Because eventually Paul writes something even more disturbing:
Those determined to become rich can fall into temptation, a trap, and harmful desires that plunge people toward ruin.
Read that carefully.
Paul is not condemning diligent work.
He is not condemning wise saving.
He is not condemning business.
He is not condemning productivity.
He is exposing what happens when “I would like to provide well” quietly mutates into “I must become rich.”
There is a difference.
One can kneel before God.
The other can become a god.
And sometimes nobody notices the moment ambition crosses the line.
You still attend church.
Still quote Scripture.
Still say, “God is blessing me.”
Still thank Him publicly.
But slowly your decisions begin revolving around income instead of obedience.
You compromise because the deal is too profitable to lose.
You neglect your children because you tell yourself you are “doing it for them.”
You stop resting because every unused hour feels like lost money.
You stop giving because generosity feels like subtraction.
You envy people you used to celebrate.
You resent people who advance faster.
You begin evaluating human beings by their usefulness to your ambitions.
Prayer becomes mostly asking God to bless plans you already made without Him.
And eventually Jesus becomes less like Lord...
and more like the divine signature you want at the bottom of your financial strategy.
That is not prosperity.
That is bondage wearing expensive clothes.
Perhaps this is why money exposes us so powerfully.
Give a person more resources and suddenly you may see what they love.
What they fear.
What they worship.
What they believe will protect them.
What they think makes them important.
Who they remember.
And who they forget.
Imagine receiving tomorrow the financial breakthrough you have been praying for.
The deposit clears.
The business explodes.
The promotion arrives.
The debt disappears.
Your income doubles.
Then triples.
What happens next?
Does generosity increase?
Does worship deepen?
Does gratitude become louder?
Does your family receive more of your presence?
Do people in need become more visible?
Does the kingdom of God become more important?
Or do your desires simply become more expensive?
That question hurts.
Because many of us want God to increase our resources without asking Him to increase our surrender.
We want a bigger harvest without a deeper altar.
But Paul refuses to leave wealthy believers trapped in guilt.
This is where the passage becomes extraordinarily beautiful.
In 1 Timothy 6:17 he addresses “those who are rich in this present age.”
And what does he tell them?
Throw everything away?
Despise every possession?
Feel ashamed every time they enjoy something?
No.
Instead, they are warned against arrogance and against placing hope in the uncertainty of wealth. Their hope belongs in God, who richly provides.
Then comes a remarkable phrase in Greek:
“πλουτεῖν ἐν ἔργοις καλοῖς.”
Ploutein en ergois kalois.
Be rich in good works.
Paul takes the concept of wealth and redeems the vocabulary.
You want to be rich?
Then become rich where heaven keeps the accounting.
Rich in generosity.
Rich in mercy.
Rich in kindness.
Rich in obedience.
Rich in good works.
Rich in willingness to share.
Rich in a life that recognizes everything ultimately belongs to God.
The passage goes on to describe believers as generous and ready to share.
That means Christianity does not merely ask:
“How much money did you make?”
It asks:
“What did your money become in the hands of a surrendered disciple?”
Did it become food?
Did it become shelter?
Did it become education?
Did it become ministry?
Did it become encouragement?
Did it become relief for somebody who thought nobody saw them?
Did it become a resource that helped someone encounter the Gospel?
Did it become an idol?
Or did it become an instrument?
And there is another detail we should not miss.
Paul says God richly provides things “for enjoyment.”
That destroys another distortion.
Biblical stewardship is not a command to feel guilty whenever God gives something good.
Gratitude is holy.
Enjoyment received with thanksgiving can honor the Giver.
The problem begins when we fall in love with the gift and slowly forget the Giver.
God does not need your money.
He already owns everything.
What He wants is you.
And perhaps that is why Jesus spoke about money so piercingly.
“Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
Your spending can become a spiritual diagnostic.
Your bank statement cannot tell the entire story of your soul, but it can sometimes ask uncomfortable questions.
What receives your first attention?
What receives your sacrifice?
What can you always afford when you want it badly enough?
What generosity do you continually postpone?
What purchase do you believe will finally make you feel significant?
What financial loss would make you question whether God is still good?
And then comes the hardest question:
If Jesus asked for something you desperately wanted to keep, would He still be Lord?
This is where the Gospel must enter the conversation.
Because Christianity is not ultimately a budgeting system.
It is not “five principles for becoming financially successful.”
It is not a baptized strategy for getting rich.
At the center of Christianity stands Jesus Christ.
And Jesus did not come merely to improve your financial circumstances.
He came to rescue sinners.
Our deepest debt was never sitting on a credit-card statement.
It was sin.
We owed what we could never repay.
No salary could erase it.
No business could outperform it.
No charitable donation could purchase forgiveness.
No amount of generosity could make a sinner righteous before a holy God.
Then Christ came.
The Son of God took on flesh.
He lived without sin.
He went to the cross.
He bore judgment sinners deserved.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
Grace accomplished what money never could.
Your greatest treasure cannot be purchased because Jesus purchased redemption at a price you could never pay.
That changes everything.
Now generosity is no longer an attempt to buy God's love.
It becomes a response to love already demonstrated at the cross.
Contentment is no longer pretending we do not need anything.
It becomes confidence that our deepest need has already been met in Christ.
Stewardship is no longer merely managing “my money.”
It becomes managing resources temporarily entrusted to me by the King.
And success is no longer having enough possessions to make people envy your life.
Success becomes hearing Christ and obeying Him.
Maybe your financial story has not been beautiful.
Maybe there is shame attached to it.
Bad decisions.
Greed.
Debt.
Dishonesty.
Impulse purchases.
Years wasted chasing status.
Money you should have given.
Money you should never have spent.
People you hurt because ambition mattered more.
Promises you made to God when you were desperate and forgot when things improved.
Maybe money became your secret security.
Maybe you discovered that your identity rises and falls with the balance in your account.
That is the scandal.
But scandal does not have to be the final chapter.
Grace can rewrite what greed wrote.
Jesus receives repentant sinners.
Repentance does not mean merely feeling guilty about money.
It means turning.
“Lord, this is Yours.”
My income.
My ambition.
My business.
My career.
My future.
My possessions.
My plans.
My fear.
My hunger for approval.
My desire to be seen as successful.
My obsession with having more.
All of it.
Yours.
And maybe the miracle you need tonight is not first a larger bank account.
Maybe it is a liberated heart.
Maybe you have been praying:
“God, increase my income.”
And tonight another prayer needs to come first:
“Jesus, increase Your rule over me.”
Because if Christ has your heart, He can teach you how to handle little.
And if Christ has your heart, He can teach you how to handle much.
Paul eventually describes generosity as laying hold of what is “truly life.”
That phrase is devastating in the best possible way.
Because there is a counterfeit version of life constantly being sold to us.
Buy this.
Earn this.
Own this.
Reach this level.
Look successful.
Make people jealous.
Upgrade again.
Then you will finally be living.
Paul looks straight through that illusion.
There is a life that only looks like life.
And there is life that is truly life.
Jesus is not asking you to trade joy for misery.
He is calling you away from the miserable task of asking money to do what money was never powerful enough to accomplish.
Money can purchase a bed.
It cannot guarantee peace.
Money can purchase medicine.
It cannot purchase immortality.
Money can purchase attention.
It cannot purchase genuine love.
Money can purchase experiences.
It cannot purchase reconciliation with God.
Money can make people know your name.
It cannot write your name in the Book of Life.
Only Jesus saves.
So keep working.
Work honestly.
Build wisely.
Provide faithfully.
Save prudently.
Give generously.
Enjoy God's gifts gratefully.
And if God entrusts you with greater wealth, receive greater stewardship with trembling gratitude.
But never ask money to become your Messiah.
It cannot carry that weight.
And perhaps now you understand why your prayer for “more” deserves another question beside it.
Not merely:
“God, will You give me more?”
But:
“God, what would more reveal about me?”
Would it reveal generosity?
Or greed?
Gratitude?
Or entitlement?
Humility?
Or superiority?
Stewardship?
Or ownership?
Faith?
Or a heart that had secretly been waiting for enough money to stop needing God?
Do not run from that question.
Bring it to Jesus.
Not because typing words saves you.
Christ saves.
But sometimes publicly acknowledging the battle is the first crack in the wall we have spent years constructing around it.
Someone reading silently may desperately need to discover that they are not the only person fighting this battle.
And please do not keep this article trapped on this page.
Not as a performance of spirituality. Not because sharing an article earns favor with God. It does not.
Come back to it the next time comparison starts whispering that everybody else is ahead of you.
Come back when ambition becomes restless.
Come back when God blesses you financially.
Especially then.
If you want to glorify God through the resources He has entrusted to you, one legitimate way to do that is to support sound Gospel work that bears good fruit. Your sharing matters too.
And there is more available for those serious about growing.
But before you leave, I want you to imagine something.
One day you will stand before Jesus without your salary.
Without your house.
Without your business.
Without your brand.
Without your investments.
Without the possessions that once made you feel successful.
You will bring none of them through eternity's door.
And on that day, you will finally see with perfect clarity what was treasure...
and what was merely expensive.
So perhaps tonight the prayer is no longer simply:
“Lord, give me more.”
Perhaps it becomes:

“Lord Jesus, whether You entrust me with little or much, do not let anything You place in my hands take the place in my heart that belongs only to You. Teach me contentment without laziness, ambition without idolatry, enjoyment without worshiping the gift, stewardship without pride, and generosity without applause. If You give me more, make me more useful to Your kingdom. If You ask me to wait, make me faithful while I wait. And if money has become my security, expose it, forgive me, and teach me again that You are enough.”
Because the greatest financial tragedy would not be reaching the end of your life without becoming rich.
It would be becoming rich...
and discovering that somewhere along the way, money became precious to you while Jesus became optional.

Do not merely ask God to enlarge what is in your hands. Ask Him to transform what is in your heart—because eventually, what is in your heart will decide what you do with everything He puts in your hands.
